newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy wakes to EMU challenge, can budget deliver?.
newsitem.headline: Italy wakes to EMU challenge, can budget deliver?.

text.p: Italy's government has belatedly realised there are no soft options if it wants to join Europe's single currency club as a founder but even a hefty dose of budget medicine may be too little, too late, commentators say.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government is engaged in a final frenzy of activity as it readies the text of a budget plan which it hopes to make public on Friday.

Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi hinted on Wednesday that the budget would try to prune the 1997 deficit by more than 32.4 trillion lire ($21.2 billion) but said press reports that a 40 trillion lire package was in the making were exaggerated.
He also said in an interview with the Rome daily La Repubblica that an overshoot of 10 to 11 trillion lire in the government's 1996 deficit target was now all but inevitable.
That meant that on top of the budget, an additional dose of fiscal tightening would be needed in 1997 to keep alive Italy's hopes of joining a currency union by 1999.
Italian newspapers have reported that an extra "tax on Europe" could be levied early next year, bringing in up to 20 trillion lire.
Economic analysts say even that would still leave Italy well short of the three percent deficit-to-GDP target which must be reached by the end of 1997 to qualify for the advance EMU party.
Current government forecasts predict Italy's deficit/GDP ratio will be 4.52 percent next year and 2.99 percent in 1998.

"The chances of meeting the (EMU) target are about 10 percent even if the government imposed a fiscal tightening of the kind we have never seen before," said Giovanna Mossetti, economist at Milan brokerage Caboto.

Ciampi left no one in any doubt over the titanic scale of the challenge Italy faces when he said on Wednesday that Italy was expected to finish the current year with a public sector deficit equivalent to 6.5 percent of GDP.
Others are even less charitable about government chances of hitting the targets set out in the Maastricht treaty on time.

"How can you cut the deficit from 6.5 percent (of GDP) to three percent in one year when the economy is practically in recession?" asked an economist at the London office of an international investment bank who requested not to be named.

Prodi is in no mood even to suggest the task might be beyond Italy's powers. "There is no doubt that the Italian government will present a budget that will put Italy in Europe (EMU)," Prodi said on a trip to the Netherlands on Tuesday.

But the spectre of failure clearly haunts Prodi, who sees the prospect of early EMU membership delivering a fat dividend in the form of lower interest rates needed to alleviate the crushing burden of servicing Italy's huge public debt.
Prodi said that for Italy to be left out of the group of EMU founding fathers would have devastating consequences.
"(It) means the economic ruin of Italy and I will certainly not be the prime minister who leaves Italy, a founding member of Europe, outside the new European union," he said.
Government hopes that Italy could secure a ticket for the departing EMU train just by showing that it was moving towards the three percent threshold are fading fast.
Some economists say Italy could conceivably make the EMU appointment on time if interest rates were to fall much faster than expected in the year ahead.
"But what you have to verify is how far are financial markets prepared to believe it," said Mario Noera, chief economist at Deutsche Bank in Milan.
Noera said that a sharp fiscal tightening would have to be compensated for by a looser monetary policy which could allow interest rates to fall sharply.
